sources.title: Andrew Gelman, John Carlin, Hal Stern, David Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed.
sources.locator: §1.3 (printed pp. 6–8), §2.5, subheading “Posterior predictive distribution” (printed p. 41), and §9.1, general decision framework (printed pp. 237–238).

contents.name: §1.3 Bayesian inference: posterior predictive distribution as a posterior average
contents.argument: The source's mixture equation averages the future-observation law over the posterior; the local definition states the probability-kernel version.

contents.name: §2.5 Posterior predictive distribution: predictive mean and two variance components
contents.argument: The source expands conditional moments and separates model sampling variance from posterior parameter uncertainty; the local theorem proves the general kernel identity under an integrated finite-second-moment condition.

contents.name: §9.1 Bayesian decision analysis: expected utility and action choice
contents.argument: The source motivates choosing actions by expected utility; the local definition fixes nonnegative loss, finite posterior risk, measurable action rules, and attained minima without assuming generic existence.

contents.name: §9.1 Decision-tree and utility examples
contents.reason: These applied decision-tree examples require domain-specific outcomes and utilities beyond the general posterior-kernel, credible-set, and Bayes-action claims assigned to this pair.

contents.name: §9.1 Finite-class actions under posterior expected loss
contents.argument: The section frames action choice through posterior expected loss. The local proof computes the finite zero–one risk as one minus the action mass and proves a deterministic measurable tie rule; no general minimizer-existence claim is imported.

contents.name: §2.5 Two-point illustration of the predictive variance decomposition
contents.argument: The source gives the predictive mean and variance decomposition; the local finite example explicitly evaluates both sides for a two-point posterior and degenerate conditional future laws.

contents.name: §9.1 A finite asymmetric-loss action comparison
contents.argument: The section motivates action choice through expected utility/loss. The false-positive and false-negative costs and all posterior-risk arithmetic in this finite example are local calculations.

sources.title: Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!: An Introduction to Applied Bayesian Modeling
sources.locator: Chapter 8 §§8.1–8.3 and §8.5; Exercise 8.8 on highest-posterior-density intervals.

contents.name: §8.1 Posterior estimation and credible intervals
contents.argument: The source defines posterior credible intervals by posterior mass and describes equal-tailed percentile intervals; the local definition uses graph measurability for a general posterior kernel.

contents.name: §8.1 Middle-percentile and highest-posterior-density intervals
contents.argument: The source distinguishes middle quantiles from a highest-density construction; the local proof verifies the equal-tailed interval's at-least-mass guarantee and the page records density and shape caveats for HPD regions.

contents.name: §8.2.2 A continuous singleton has posterior probability zero
contents.argument: The source computes zero posterior mass for a point under a continuous posterior. The local Beta(2,2) example turns this into the exact-zero-one point-action risk calculation.

contents.name: §8.3 Posterior predictive model as a posterior-weighted mixture
contents.argument: The source averages a conditional predictive distribution over posterior uncertainty; the local result proves the mixture is a measurable probability kernel and gives its nonnegative integral identity.

contents.name: §8.3 Posterior and sampling variability in future predictions
contents.argument: The source describes both posterior variability and future sampling variability; the local theorem gives the exact mean and variance formulas for arbitrary scalar future kernels.

contents.name: §8.1 Posterior quantiles and middle-percentile intervals
contents.argument: The text uses posterior quantiles to form middle-percentile intervals; the local lemma fixes the rational lower-quantile convention and proves measurability and the CDF bracket for arbitrary measurable posterior kernels.

contents.name: §8.1 Equal-tailed interval endpoints as posterior quantiles
contents.argument: A posterior median is the one-half quantile; the local lemma proves that this lower-quantile selection is measurable and satisfies both half-mass inequalities on every data fiber.

contents.name: §8.3 Posterior predictive variance with parameter uncertainty
contents.argument: The text separates future sampling variability from posterior variability; the local two-point Bernoulli example computes an exact case where the latter supplies the whole predictive variance.

contents.name: §8.5 Posterior and frequentist conditioning answer different questions
contents.argument: The text distinguishes posterior probabilities conditioning on observed data from frequentist probabilities conditioning on a fixed parameter. The local uniform-prior Bernoulli calculation derives a central 95% interval whose frequentist coverage is zero at the stated parameter; the source does not claim an interval-coverage theorem.

sources.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory
sources.locator: §5.3.1, Definition 5.3 and Example 5.4, including the following absolute-error-loss paragraph, printed pp. 104–105.

contents.name: Definition 5.3 Bayes risk and posterior risk by iterated integration
contents.argument: The source identifies posterior risk as expected loss under the posterior and notes its relation to prior-averaged risk; the local definition states finite-integral, measurable-selection, and attainment requirements.

contents.name: Example 5.4 Squared-error posterior risk minimized by the posterior mean
contents.argument: The source expands squared posterior risk; the local proof uses the published L² projection theorem, preserving its AC assumption and proving measurability on the finite-second-moment data domain.

contents.name: Example 5.4 Absolute-error posterior risk minimized by a posterior median
contents.argument: The source states the median action; the local proof compares all actions directly and supplies a measurable lower-median selector.

contents.name: Example 5.5 Composite two-hypothesis zero–one test and tie randomization
contents.reason: This example is a composite testing problem with a randomized tie rule; the assigned theorem concerns deterministic posterior-mass maximizers on a finite class and makes no composite-test or randomization claim.

contents.name: Example 5.4 Posterior medians under absolute loss
contents.argument: The source identifies posterior medians as absolute-loss actions; the local definition specifies the two closed-side half-mass inequalities, including discrete and mixed laws.

contents.name: Example 5.4 Measurable lower-median selector
contents.argument: The source motivates median actions but supplies no measurable kernel selector; the local result obtains one from the lower posterior quantile and checks both median inequalities.

contents.name: Example 5.4 Nonunique median finite witness
contents.argument: The source states the median action principle; the local two-atom posterior verifies directly that every action between the atoms is a median with risk one-half.

contents.name: Example 5.4 Asymmetric-loss comparison
contents.argument: The source introduces posterior risk as expected loss. The example's asymmetric costs and posterior risk comparison are original finite arithmetic, not a quoted source example.

contents.name: Example 5.5 Composite two-hypothesis test and randomized tie rule
contents.reason: This source example tests a composite null against an alternative and randomizes at a tie. The assigned theorem is instead a choice-free deterministic selector for a maximal-mass action on an arbitrary finite class, so the testing and randomization assumptions are not transferred.

sources.inspection: Read the full lecture-notes PDF at §5.3.1, including the posterior-risk formula, squared-error calculation, absolute-error median statement, and neighboring finite two-hypothesis example.
